title: The master and the leg
hook: enslaved, Epictetus warns his master he'll break his leg, it breaks, and he says calmly "didn't I tell you?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus Aurelius: the emperor arguing with his blankets. Your line was up, to do a human's work. Did you get up at the first alarm? Day twenty-three.

Yesterday an emperor. Today, a man at the very bottom of the same empire. He was born in a town in what's now Turkey, and he was born enslaved. The only name we have for him, Epictetus, is a Greek word for acquired. Bought. His owner was a wealthy man in Rome, himself a former slave of the emperor Nero's household. And one day, so the story goes, the owner starts twisting Epictetus's leg. Hard. For no reason we're told. And Epictetus, instead of crying out, looks at him and speaks.
screen: `THE BOTTOM OF THE SAME EMPIRE.` → `HIS NAME MEANS ACQUIRED.` → `THE MASTER TWISTS HIS LEG.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as it comes down to us. Epictetus says, quietly: you're going to break it. The master keeps twisting. The leg breaks. And Epictetus says, calmly: didn't I tell you it would break? That's it. No scream, no curse. Now, honesty about the source. This story isn't from Epictetus himself. It comes from an ancient writer named Celsus, who told it in a book attacking Christianity, and we only have it because a Christian scholar, Origen, quoted Celsus in order to answer him. Another ancient source says Epictetus's lameness came from illness, not cruelty. So we can't be sure it happened. But we know Epictetus was lame, and we know what he taught about it. In George Long's translation of his handbook: "Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will." And the handbook's first line: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." A twisted leg is not in your power, if someone stronger is doing the twisting. What you say while it happens, that part may still be yours. Please hear what this story doesn't mean. It doesn't mean cruelty is fine, or that pain doesn't hurt, or that someone being harmed should just keep quiet. If it happened, it was wrong. The story is about something smaller and stranger: that even at the very bottom, with no power at all, a person can still choose the voice they answer in. Epictetus spent the rest of his life teaching that.
screen: `YOU'RE GOING TO BREAK IT.` · `A STORY TOLD BY A CRITIC.` · `IMPEDIMENT TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.` · `CRUELTY IS STILL WRONG.` · then, large: `THE VOICE YOU ANSWER IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then gently notice one pain you can't change today. A sore back. A diagnosis. A person who won't change. A loss. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just let it be there, and breathe beside it. Then ask quietly: what part of this is mine? Maybe only the voice you answer it in. Rest with that for a while. If it's too much today, just come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus. An enslaved man, a broken leg, and a calm answer: didn't I tell you?
Your line: said calmly. Today, when something you can't change goes wrong, notice the voice you answer in. Choose it, once. Day twenty-three.

howItsDone: Stoic practice sorts troubles into what is in our power and what is not, and puts effort only into the first: our own judgments, choices and responses.

original.note: Greek: acquired, gained. The name of an enslaved man who became a teacher of philosophy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tough guy who didn't feel pain.
what it means: a man with no power choosing the voice he answers in.
what a scholar hears: Celsus in Origen, Against Celsus 7.53; the Suda attributes his lameness to rheumatism; Enchiridion 9 separates the leg from the will.

sources.quoted: Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.
Of things some are in our power, and others are not.

notes: Long 1877: confirm exact wording of Enchiridion 9 ('Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.') and Enchiridion 1 ('Of things some are in our power, and others are not.').
Epictetus born c. 50–55 CE in Hierapolis, Phrygia; master Epaphroditus, a freedman in Nero's service. Confirm.
Name: ἐπίκτητος means 'acquired'; that his birth name is unknown is standard. Confirm.
The dialogue ('you're going to break it' / 'didn't I tell you it would break?') is paraphrased from Celsus via Origen 7.53; the hook's quotation marks come from the index.
The Suda says lameness from rheumatism; script says 'illness'.
Script explicitly says cruelty was wrong and the story isn't a call to silence under harm.

Review 2026-10-01: removed the birth year and the unsourced claim that his birth name is lost; Celsus no longer dated; 'lame all his life' (not in any cited source) became 'lame', in the teach and the myth; dropped 'famous'; 'the leg was broken' now 'if it happened, it was wrong', matching the script's own doubt about the story; dropped 'one of the great teachers' from the original note.
